---
title: "Preparing TerraClimate"
subtitle: "Monthly precipitation and PET, from yearly downloads to a single SPI/SPEI-ready file"
---

## What TerraClimate is

TerraClimate is a global monthly climate and climatic water balance dataset at
**1/24 degree, about 4 km**, running from **1950 to the present**. It is built by
climatically aided interpolation: high-resolution climatological normals from
WorldClim are combined with coarser time-varying fields from reanalysis, so it
keeps the spatial detail of the normals and the year-to-year variability of the
reanalysis.

Two of its variables matter here, and **which you need depends on the index**:

| Variable | What it is | Units | SPI | SPEI |
|:---|:---|:---|:--:|:--:|
| `ppt` | Accumulated precipitation | mm | required | required |
| `pet` | Reference evapotranspiration, ASCE Penman-Monteith | mm | not used | required |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Only want SPI? Download `ppt` and stop

SPI is computed from precipitation alone. If SPEI is not on your list, skip
`pet` entirely: you download **11.6 GB instead of 19.8 GB**, and steps 2 and 3
below halve.

The rest of this page applies unchanged. Wherever it says "both variables",
read "your one variable".
:::

The files carry their own provenance. Version 1.1 records `source: WorldClim
v2.1, ERA5` and this reference:

> Abatzoglou, J.T., Hegewisch, K.C., Yin, C. and D.A. Kalashinkov, 2026,
> TerraClimate v1.1, An Updated Global Climate and Climatic Water Balance
> Dataset with Climate Scenarios. Scientific Data.

The dataset [landing page](https://www.climatologylab.org/terraclimate.html)
cites the original v1 paper, Abatzoglou et al. 2018, for the method. Cite the
version you actually used, and read it out of the file rather than trusting your
notes:

```python
import xarray as xr
with xr.open_dataset("TerraClimate_ppt_2024.nc") as ds:
    print(ds.attrs["version"], "|", ds.attrs["references"])
```

::: {.callout-note}
## The scripts on this page

The helper functions used below live in `docs/tutorials/scripts/tc_prepare.py`,
and the packing check is `docs/tutorials/scripts/check_packing.py`. The imports
shown assume you are working from `docs/tutorials/`; adjust the path or copy the
module next to your own code.
:::

### Naming convention

One file per variable per year, always:

```
TerraClimate_{variable}_{yyyy}.nc
```

So `TerraClimate_ppt_1950.nc` through `TerraClimate_ppt_2025.nc`, and the same
for `pet`. Each yearly file holds twelve monthly steps on the full
4,320 x 8,640 global grid.

---

## Step 1: Download

### Individually

Browse the [THREDDS
catalog](http://thredds.northwestknowledge.net:8080/thredds/catalog/TERRACLIMATE_ALL/data/catalog.html)
and click through. Note that this server is plain HTTP on port 8080, so some
clients that force HTTPS will fail to reach it.

### In bulk

Direct downloads come from `climate.northwestknowledge.net` over HTTPS.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Windows (cmd)

```bat
for /L %y in (1950, 1, 2025) do C:\apps\gnuwin64\wget.exe ^
  "https://climate.northwestknowledge.net/TERRACLIMATE-DATA/TerraClimate_ppt_%y.nc" -c

for /L %y in (1950, 1, 2025) do C:\apps\gnuwin64\wget.exe ^
  "https://climate.northwestknowledge.net/TERRACLIMATE-DATA/TerraClimate_pet_%y.nc" -c
```

The second loop fetches `pet` and is only needed for SPEI. Skip it for SPI.

If you do not have `wget`, install it with `winget install GnuWin32.Wget` or
take the binary from [GnuWin](https://sourceforge.net/projects/gnuwin64/).

In a `.bat` file use `%%y` instead of `%y`.

#### Linux / macOS

```bash
# For SPI only, drop pet from this list.
for v in ppt pet; do
  for y in $(seq 1950 2025); do
    wget -c "https://climate.northwestknowledge.net/TERRACLIMATE-DATA/TerraClimate_${v}_${y}.nc"
  done
done
```

#### Python

Resumes part-downloads, skips files already complete, and fails loudly on a
truncated file instead of leaving one to break the merge later.

```python
from pathlib import Path
from scripts.tc_prepare import download_year

VARIABLES = ("ppt", "pet")     # ("ppt",) is enough for SPI

for var in VARIABLES:
    for year in range(1950, 2026):
        download_year(var, year, Path("raw"))
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Use `-c`, not `--no-check-certificate`

`-c` resumes a partial download, and the server supports it: it returns
`Accept-Ranges: bytes`. Restarting a 150 MB file from zero because the
connection dropped at 90% is the main thing that makes this step painful.

You may see `--no-check-certificate` in older recipes for this host. It disables
certificate verification, which is a real security downgrade. Try without it
first; HTTPS to this host verifies correctly as of this writing.
:::

### How much you are downloading

Measured from the server's `Content-Length` headers:

| | Per year | 76 years (1950-2025) | Needed for |
|:---|---:|---:|:---|
| `ppt` | ~152 MB | **~11.6 GB** | SPI and SPEI |
| `pet` | ~108 MB | **~8.2 GB** | SPEI only |
| Both | | **~19.8 GB** | SPEI |

---

## Step 2: Unpack

This is the step that is easy to skip and expensive to get wrong.

TerraClimate is distributed as [packed
data](https://cfconventions.org/Data/cf-conventions/cf-conventions-1.7/build/ch08.html):
the values on disk are integers, and the CF attributes `scale_factor` and
`add_offset` tell a reader how to turn them back into millimetres. It is a
sensible way to ship a large dataset, and it is not a sensible way to keep one
you are about to compute on.

Here is what the two variables actually look like upstream, read from the
THREDDS metadata by `scripts/check_packing.py`:

| File | dtype | `scale_factor` | `_FillValue` |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| `TerraClimate_ppt_1950.nc` | `int32` | 0.1 | −2147483648 |
| `TerraClimate_ppt_1990.nc` | `int32` | 0.1 | −2147483648 |
| `TerraClimate_ppt_2024.nc` | `int32` | 0.1 | −2147483648 |
| `TerraClimate_pet_1950.nc` | `int16` | 0.1 | −32768 |
| `TerraClimate_pet_2024.nc` | `int16` | 0.1 | −32768 |

Two things to take from that table.

**The packing is stable across years within a variable.** Both `ppt` and `pet`
use the same scale factor in every year checked, so concatenating them will not
silently rescale part of your series. That is worth confirming rather than
assuming, because it is not guaranteed by anything, and the failure would be
invisible.

**The two variables are packed differently from each other.** `ppt` is `int32`
with a fill of −2147483648; `pet` is `int16` with a fill of −32768. Any code
that hardcodes one fill value, or that does arithmetic on the raw integers, is
wrong for one of them.

### Why this matters in practice

If a reader applies `scale_factor` but not the fill mask, the ocean does not
become NaN. It becomes a number:

| Variable | Fill, unpacked naively | Looks like |
|:---|---:|:---|
| `ppt` | −214,748,364.8 mm | Obviously broken |
| `pet` | **−3,276.8 mm** | Plausible enough to survive a sanity check |

The `pet` case is the dangerous one. A range check that rejects absurd
magnitudes will catch the precipitation error and wave the PET error through,
and you will find out much later when a water balance somewhere is wrong by
3,276 mm.

xarray does the right thing by default, `mask_and_scale=True`. Plenty of other
tools do not, and neither does anything that reads the integers directly.
Unpacking once, at the start, removes the question from every later step.

### Doing it

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### NCO

```bash
# one file
ncpdq --unpack TerraClimate_ppt_1950.nc ppt/TerraClimate_ppt_1950.nc

# all files, Linux/macOS
for f in TerraClimate_ppt_*.nc; do ncpdq --unpack "$f" "ppt/$f"; done

# all files, Windows cmd
for %f in (TerraClimate_ppt_*.nc) do ncpdq --unpack "%f" "ppt\%f"
```

#### Python

```python
from pathlib import Path
from scripts.tc_prepare import unpack_file

for src in sorted(Path("raw").glob("TerraClimate_ppt_*.nc")):
    unpack_file(src, Path("unpacked") / src.name)
```

:::

The Python version writes `float32` with a single `_FillValue` of −9999 and
strips the packing attributes, so downstream code never sees them again.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why `float32` and not `float64`

The source is quantised at 0.1 mm. A float32 round-trip of these values is
accurate to **1.2e-05 mm**, four orders of magnitude finer than the data's own
precision, so `float64` stores no additional information about the world.

It does double your disk and your memory. For the full global series that is
136 GB against 272 GB per variable before compression. Unless you have a
specific reason, write `float32`.
:::

---

## Step 3: Merge the years

SPI and SPEI need one continuous series per variable, not 76 files.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### CDO

```bash
cdo -z zip_5 mergetime TerraClimate_ppt_*.nc wld_cli_terraclimate_ppt_1950_2025.nc
```

#### Python

```python
from pathlib import Path
from scripts.tc_prepare import merge_years

files = sorted(Path("unpacked").glob("TerraClimate_ppt_*.nc"))
merge_years(files, Path("wld_cli_terraclimate_ppt_1950_2025.nc"), var="ppt")
```

:::

Both work. The Python route is worth the extra line because it controls two
things `cdo mergetime` decides for you: the output dtype, and the on-disk chunk
shape.

::: {.callout-important}
## Chunk for how you will read it

A NetCDF chunk is the smallest unit that can be read. If the file is chunked one
month at a time across the full width of the world, then reading the full
history of one small area means touching every chunk in the file.

That is the layout `mergetime` tends to produce, and it is the opposite of what
SPI and SPEI want, because they read a complete time series per pixel.

`merge_years` defaults to a chunk that spans the whole time axis and is small
spatially, which makes a per-pixel series a single read. The trade-off is that
producing it requires rewriting the data rather than concatenating it, so the
merge takes longer and needs working space.
:::

---

## Step 4: Check before you compute

```python
import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_dataset("wld_cli_terraclimate_ppt_1950_2025.nc")
ppt = ds["ppt"]

print(f"dims   : {ppt.dims} {ppt.shape}")
print(f"dtype  : {ppt.dtype}")
print(f"time   : {str(ppt.time.values[0])[:10]} to {str(ppt.time.values[-1])[:10]}"
      f"  ({ppt.sizes['time']} steps)")
print(f"units  : {ppt.attrs.get('units')}")

# The packing must be gone, not merely applied.
leftovers = [a for a in ("scale_factor", "add_offset", "_Unsigned")
             if a in ppt.encoding or a in ppt.attrs]
print(f"packing attributes left: {leftovers or 'none'}")

# Ocean must be NaN, not a large negative number.
sample = ppt.isel(time=-1).values
print(f"finite cells : {np.isfinite(sample).sum():,} of {sample.size:,}")
print(f"min / max    : {np.nanmin(sample):.1f} / {np.nanmax(sample):.1f} mm")
assert np.nanmin(sample) >= 0, "negative precipitation: fill value leaked through"
```

For the global v1.1 series that prints 912 monthly steps from 1950-01 to
2025-12, and 12.5 million finite cells out of 37.3 million, which is the 33.6%
of the grid that is land.

---

## Smaller areas

Everything above produces the **global** grid. If your area of interest is a
bounding box, a country or a custom shapefile, subset after unpacking and before
merging, which saves both time and disk.

See [Preparing Your Data](00-data-preparation.qmd) for subsetting, coordinate
naming, and the rest of the input contract.

---

## What you should have

For SPEI, two files:

```
wld_cli_terraclimate_ppt_1950_2025.nc     ppt, float32, (912, 4320, 8640)
wld_cli_terraclimate_pet_1950_2025.nc     pet, float32, (912, 4320, 8640)
```

For SPI, just the first. Either way: unpacked, NaN over ocean, and if you have
both, on the same grid and the same time axis.

That is the input contract for `spi()` and `spei()`, and for the global routes
described in [Implementation](../technical/implementation.qmd).

---

## TerraClimate or CHIRPS for SPI?

Both will give you SPI. They differ in ways that are measurable, and the choice
is usually decided by the first two rows:

| | TerraClimate v1.1 | CHIRPS v3.0 |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Record starts | **1950** | 1981 |
| Coverage | All land, lat -89.98 to 89.98 | **60S-60N only** |
| Resolution | 1/24 degree, ~4 km | 0.05 degree, ~5 km |
| Grid | 4,320 x 8,640 | 2,400 x 7,200 |
| Release unit | One file per **year** | One file per **month** |
| **Latency** | **The current year is absent entirely** | **10-13 days after month end** |
| Download for SPI | ~11.6 GB | ~8.9 GB |
| Packed on disk | Yes, unpack first | No |
| Construction | WorldClim normals + ERA5 reanalysis | Infrared satellite estimates with station data |

The length of record matters for a 30-year calibration: 1950 leaves 46 years
outside the baseline where 1981 leaves 15. And if your area is above 60N or
below 60S, CHIRPS does not cover it at all.

Latency pulls the other way, and it pulls hard.

::: {.callout-important}
## TerraClimate is not an operational monitoring dataset

TerraClimate is released one file per calendar year, and the current year is
not published at all while it is running. Checked on **2026-09-29**:

| | Newest available |
|:--|:--|
| TerraClimate | **2025** (`TerraClimate_ppt_2026.nc` returns 404) |
| CHIRPS | **August 2026**, published 11 September, 10 days after month end |

That is a **13-month** difference in how current your index can be, today.

CHIRPS publication latency measured over the last four months: 11, 13, 13 and
10 days after the month ends. Reproduce with
`scripts/check_latency.py`.

So:

- **Monitoring a current drought** needs CHIRPS, or another
  low-latency product. TerraClimate cannot answer "what is happening now".
- **Studying the historical record**, fitting distributions, computing
  climatologies or looking at multi-decade trends, is where TerraClimate's
  extra 31 years earns its place.
- **SPEI at all** needs TerraClimate or an equivalent PET source, since CHIRPS
  publishes precipitation only.

A common arrangement is both: TerraClimate for the baseline and the long
record, CHIRPS for the near-real-time update.
:::

There is no need to choose permanently. The two are on different grids, so
compare them as separate runs rather than trying to merge them. See
[Preparing CHIRPS](00a-chirps.qmd) for that route.
